## The phrase you played before [Lesson 1](../00-getting-a-sound-out/01-hello-sound.qmd)

`[:e4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :d5, :b4, :a4, :g4]`. You ran that in the setup buffer,
before any of this started: eight symbols and a sleep. E minor pentatonic over
an E2 bass, picked so nothing could clash while you found Run.

Those eight pitches carry all three capstones: a solo melody here, an
accompaniment in [Lesson 56](56-capstone-b-melody-accompaniment.qmd), two voices in [Lesson 57](57-capstone-c-two-voice-polyphony.qmd). Nothing new gets invented,
which is the point. Fifty-four lessons went into describing music, and here's
where you find out what that bought you. Same eight notes. Much more to say
about them.

Two layers, two jobs. An event list records pitch, start, duration, dynamics,
articulation and phrase as evidence. A renderer decides how Sonic Pi presents
it. Measure references ride along, so a disputed claim leads back to its bar.

## Eight notes with a shape and a peak

Four bars, built as a *period*: an antecedent that ends unresolved, a consequent
that answers it. Both open with the same four notes. Phrase `:a` stops on G4,
hanging. Phrase `:b` lands on E4. One changed note, and that's the difference
between a question and an answer.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 74
use_synth :piano

score = [
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :e4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.58, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :g4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.62, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :a4, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.66, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :b4, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.72, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :d5, start: 4.0, duration: 2.0, amp: 0.80, articulation: :accent},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :b4, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.70, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :g4, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.62, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 3, phrase: :b, note: :e4, start: 8.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.60, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 3, phrase: :b, note: :g4, start: 9.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.65, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 3, phrase: :b, note: :a4, start: 10.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.70, articulation: :detached},
  {measure: 3, phrase: :b, note: :b4, start: 11.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.76, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 4, phrase: :b, note: :d5, start: 12.0, duration: 2.0, amp: 0.90, articulation: :accent},
  {measure: 4, phrase: :b, note: :b4, start: 14.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.74, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 4, phrase: :b, note: :e4, start: 15.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.60, articulation: :legato}
]

define :play_events do |events|
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    release_ratio = event[:articulation] == :detached ? 0.48 : 0.9
    accent_gain = event[:articulation] == :accent ? 0.12 : 0.0
    play event[:note],
      release: event[:duration] * release_ratio,
      amp: event[:amp] + accent_gain
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

play_events score
```

D5 arrives twice, and the second is louder. Pitch marks the ceiling, amplitude
marks bar 4 as the climax, and the line falls away to E. You can't tell from the
data whether that intention reaches a listener.

The detached A4 in bar 3 shortens only its release. Its notated duration still
fills a beat, so B4 arrives at 11.0 as before. Score timeline and audible length
stay separate: [Lesson 7](../01-why-sound-has-structure/07-envelope-instrument.qmd)'s distinction, turning up where it matters.

## Flatten the dynamics, then the accent

1. Set every `amp` to 0.7. The contour still reaches D5 twice, and it doesn't
   tell you which arrival matters. Where did those numbers come from: source
   markings, or choices you made?
2. Restore the amplitudes and change the bar-4 D5 from `:accent` to `:legato`.
   Still highest, still loudest, softer attack. That splits structural
   importance from one performer's emphasis.
3. Add `source_time` to every event and a `REVIEW` field to a note you doubt.
   Print them before playback. No sound changes; you gain a path from any event
   back to its evidence.

## What one schema lets every tool share

One event shape means every tool agrees about the same score. Bar checks read
starts and durations. Range reports read notes. The renderer reads articulation
and amplitude. Provenance reads measures. No helper needs its own
representation for one awkward phrase.

Absolute starts make gaps and overlaps visible and stop an early mistake
shifting every later coordinate. Phrase labels give a formal view without
duplicating events into section arrays. When a repeated phrase returns varied,
store the new events and label the relationship. An alias would claim they're
identical. Here `:a` and `:b` share six notes and part company on the seventh.

Review at more than one scale. Validate every bar, loop each phrase against its
source, step back for the whole contour, then hear the expressive rendering end
to end. A pitch can be locally right while the phrase is wrong.

## Take the phrase to thirty-two bars

Now do it for real. Take thirty-two to sixty-four bars from your [Lesson 42](../09-transcription/42-finding-music-you-can-legally-use.qmd) list, run the [Lesson 43](../09-transcription/43-four-pass-pipeline.qmd) pipeline and the [Lesson 46](../09-transcription/46-debug-transcription-like-software.qmd) checks on a short
excerpt, then expand. Pick a source with several phrases, a clear high point,
repeated material, and one passage that resists. That resistance gives the
method real work.

Deliver a source record, a bar-by-bar validation report, global range, phrase
labels, articulation, dynamics, and every uncertain passage with source
coordinates. Then feed one score array into two renderers, strict and
expressive. Pitch and duration stay identical. Compare phrase by phrase and
account for every performance change.
